title: Cisco Secure Endpoint Threat Detections by Host
exclusions: Covers detections by the Secure Endpoint connector only, and only for event types the input collects. Quarantine outcomes and retrospective verdicts are separate searches.
evidence: Saved alert results per host with detection names, hashes, and the trajectory link, plus the incident or ticket closing each host.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Download the EICAR test file to a test host running the Secure Endpoint connector. Within one input interval a Threat Detected event (`event_type_id=1090519054`) for that host is indexed, and the search returns a row with the test host and the EICAR detection name.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Copy a clean, known file to the same host. No detection event is created and the search returns no row for the host.

dataSources: `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Secure Endpoint input, which polls `GET /v1/events`. This search uses event types 1090519054 (Threat Detected) and 1090519084 (DFC Threat Detected). Each event carries `event_type`, `event_type_id`, `detection`, `severity`, `connector_guid`, `group_guids{}`, `computer.hostname`, `computer.user`, `computer.external_ip`, `computer.links.trajectory`, and for file events `file.file_name`, `file.file_path`, `file.disposition`, and `file.identity.sha256`.
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Cisco Secure Endpoint input.
spl:
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id IN (1090519054, 1090519084)
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(event_type) as event_types values(detection) as detections values(severity) as severities values(file_name) as files values(sha256) as sha256 values(user) as users latest(trajectory) as trajectory by host_name connector_guid
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
description: Groups Cisco Secure Endpoint threat detections and Device Flow Correlation (malicious network connection) detections by host. Each row shows the detection names, severities, files and hashes involved, the users on the host, and the link to the device trajectory in the Secure Endpoint console.
value: A host-centred view tells the responder which machine to isolate first and whether the same file is spreading. The trajectory link opens the full process and file history for that host, so triage starts with context rather than a bare alert.
implementation: Collect Secure Endpoint events with the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) input into `index=secure_endpoint`. Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and alert on every row; raise to critical when a host has more than one distinct detection.
visualization: Alert table: host_name, event_types, detections, severities, files, sha256, users, count, firstTime, lastTime, trajectory. Supporting panels: detections per day by severity over 30 days (stacked column), top detection names (bar chart).

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Potentially unwanted applications** — adware and bundled installers are detected as threats with low severity. Tune by detection name after review.

2. **Security testing** — EICAR files and red-team tools trigger real detections. Keep a lookup of test hosts and exercise windows.

3. **Custom detections** — simple custom detection lists in the console flag files your own team chose; they are true positives by definition but may be low priority.

**Suppression:** throttle per host and detection for 4 hours.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs.
• A Secure Endpoint API credential: in the Secure Endpoint console under Administration > API Credentials, create a read-only credential and record the client ID and API key, plus the API host for your region (for example `api.amp.cisco.com` for North America, `api.eu.amp.cisco.com` for Europe).
• Outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the input host to the API host.
• An index for Secure Endpoint data (this page uses `index=secure_endpoint`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the SOC and endpoint teams.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Cisco Secure Endpoint card, and create an input with the API host, client ID, and API key. Set the index to `secure_endpoint`. The modular input polls `GET /v1/events` with a default interval of 300 seconds and writes `sourcetype=cisco:se`.
• Select the event types the input should collect. Collecting all types is simplest; if you limit them, include the event type IDs this search uses.
• In a distributed deployment run the input on one node only; the guide notes that the computers, compromises, and top-malware endpoints can produce duplicates otherwise.
• Check the events this search needs: run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se | stats count by event_type_id event_type` over 7 days and confirm 1090519054 appears.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=secure_endpoint sourcetype="cisco:se" event_type_id IN (1090519054, 1090519084)
| eval host_name='computer.hostname', user='computer.user', sha256='file.identity.sha256', file_name='file.file_name', file_path='file.file_path', trajectory='computer.links.trajectory'
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(event_type) as event_types values(detection) as detections values(severity) as severities values(file_name) as files values(sha256) as sha256 values(user) as users latest(trajectory) as trajectory by host_name connector_guid
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
```

Understanding this SPL
• 1090519054 is Threat Detected (a file) and 1090519084 is DFC Threat Detected (a connection to a known-bad address seen by Device Flow Correlation).
• `eval` copies the nested `computer.*` and `file.*` JSON fields into short names.
• `stats` by host and connector GUID gives one row per machine, with every detection and hash seen in the window.
• `trajectory` is the console URL for the host's device trajectory.

Step 3 — Validate
• Compare with the Secure Endpoint console Events page filtered to Threat Detected for the same time range: the counts per host should match.
• Open the `trajectory` link for one row and confirm it shows the same file and detection.
• Run `index=secure_endpoint sourcetype=cisco:se | timechart span=1h count by event_type` over 7 days; flat zero for all types for more than two intervals means the input stopped, not that the estate is clean.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and throttle on `host_name` plus `detections` for 4 hours.
• Route to the SOC. For DFC detections, check firewall and proxy logs for the same destination from other hosts.
• When Enterprise Security is in use, the Cisco Security Cloud app can also promote these event types to findings; use one path, not both, to avoid duplicate findings.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No cisco:se events and HTTP 401 in the input log: wrong client ID or API key, or the API host is for a different region from the organisation.
• Events arrive but `event_type_id` is missing: the events were indexed before JSON extraction applied; check `| fieldsummary` on one hour of data.
• Duplicate events with the same `id`: the input runs on more than one node, or the legacy AMP for Endpoints input (Splunkbase 3686) is still enabled. Keep one collector.
grandmaExplanation: The antivirus on each computer reports when it finds something bad. We group those reports by computer, so the team knows which machine to clean first.
